text: The date is off by one day, so I'll patch the formatter. Wait, the offset only appears for users east of UTC, which points at the parser. Let me check that first.
I'll wrap the whole handler in a mutex to stop the race. But the race is between two processes, so an in-process mutex never sees it. We need a lock in the store.

We can roll back the deploy from the dashboard in one click, so the risk is low. However, this release also ran a data migration, and the code rollback does not revert the rows. Let's write the down-migration first.
The mean order value jumped, so I'll report it as growth. Actually, a single bulk order is skewing the mean; the median is flat. Let me report the median.
I teach the stack with trays because the push and pop picture is immediate. That said, trays suggest copying, so I add a pointer diagram at the end to fix that.
The client should retry on timeout, and twice is plenty. However, the server is idempotent only for reads, so a write retry could double-charge. Let me add an idempotency key first.
I'll move the settings into the database so ops can change them live. Yet the app also needs those values during boot, before the database is up. A file with an env override is the smaller fix.
We can close the epic once the last subtask lands. Hold on, the acceptance criteria include a load test that was never scheduled. Let me add it before we close.

Support calls track the outage graph closely, so calls are a good outage proxy. But both are driven by the same deploy schedule, so they correlate without causing each other. I need a deploy-free period to test it.
I start loops with the counting example because every student knows it. However, counting loops hide the condition design, which is the hard part. I now open with a sentinel loop instead.

The writes are lost because the buffer is too small, so I'll raise the flush interval. Actually, the buffer flushes fine; the process is killed before the final flush runs. A shutdown hook is the fix.
One endpoint per screen is clean and easy to cache. However, three screens share the same header query, so we would fan out three calls on every route change. Let me merge the shared part.
We can absorb the overage inside this quarter's budget. Wait — the contract bills annually in advance, so the overage lands in last year's line. Let me check with finance.
Mobile conversion fell, so the redesign hurt mobile users. I realize now that the mobile share of traffic doubled, so the rate fell while counts rose. Conversion volume is up.
I explain private fields with the sealed box image because it is memorable. That said, the box image makes testing feel like a violation, so I show the friend seam too.

The slow query needs a composite index on both columns. But the planner already uses a bitmap scan on one of them and the other is low cardinality, so the index would not help. The problem is the sort.

A per-tenant quota in the gateway is the simplest throttle. On the other hand, the noisy tenant drives load from a single long-lived stream that never hits the gateway. The limit has to live in the consumer.
The audit is a good candidate for the sprint, it is mostly reading. Wait, it needs three signatures and two of the reviewers are out next week. Let's slot it after their return.
The sample is large enough that the effect is certain, so I'll call it significant. But the effect size is inside the daily noise band, so it is certain and tiny at once. That is not worth shipping.
I define big-O as the growth rate, and the graph makes it concrete. However, students then assume constants never matter, which is false for small n. I add a timing exercise to correct it.

The format string looks wrong at first glance. Wait for the locale fixture to load before judging, because the pattern is built from the locale on purpose. It renders correctly once the fixture is in place.

A mutex around the handler is cheap, but the store lock is the one that actually orders the writers, so both are worth having and neither alone is sufficient. The mutex is the front door and the store lock is the vault.

The mean is actually above the median here, which is normal for a right-skewed order distribution. Reporting both is the honest move, and the gap between them is a useful measure of how much a few large buyers move the number.

The tray picture is easy to grasp and the pointer diagram fixes its main flaw. That said, I draw both in the same slide so the students compare them side by side, and the contrast is what makes the copy-versus-reference distinction stick.

Retrying twice is fine for reads, however writes need an idempotency key before any retry policy is safe, and that key is one header on the request. The retry count is a tuning knob; the key is the correctness fix.

The database is the natural home for mutable settings, yet boot-time values must be readable before it is up, so the file plus env override stays. Both layers have a job: the file for boot, the database for the long tail of runtime knobs.
